| [LIT-056](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-056.md) v3 | Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness | Butlin et al. (2023), [ARXIV-2308.08708](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.08708). The report assumes computational functionalism and takes a "theory-heavy" approach. From it the authors derive 14 indicator properties: RPT-1–2, GWT-1–4, HOT-1–4, AST-1, PP-1 and AE-1–2. The claim for them is only that more of them raises the probability of consciousness. They assess a handful of systems against subsets of the list and conclude that no current system "appears to be a strong candidate". Transformer LLMs have "only a relatively weak case" for any GWT indicator, because a single forward pass has no recurrence or global broadcast. Perceiver arguably has GWT-1, GWT-2 and half of GWT-4 but lacks broadcast. Among the embodied agents, AdA is the likeliest to meet AE-2. Most indicators could be built with standard ML techniques. The abstract's "no current AI systems are conscious" is stronger than anything the body shows. | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-052); the reference statement of the indicator-property ("theory-heavy") approach to AI consciousness, worth reading for §1–§2 (method and theory survey) and Tables 1–2. | [LIT-096](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-096.md) | What Is It Like to Be a Bat? | Nagel (1974), [DOI-10.2307/2183914](https://doi.org/10.2307/2183914). An organism has conscious states if and only if there is something it is like to be that organism. That subjective character belongs to a type of point of view, and it is left out by every functional, intentional or causal analysis, since each is compatible with its absence. Reduction elsewhere moves away from a point of view toward the objective; here that move leads away from the thing being explained. So physicalism may be true, but we have no conception of how it could be. Nagel proposes an "objective phenomenology" that would describe experience to beings who cannot have it. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 (NOTE-089); the source of the "something it is like" criterion of consciousness that the record's AI-consciousness work (LIT-056) adopts as its target, and of the argument that no functional analysis can settle whether that criterion is met. |

| [LIT-120](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-120.md) v2 | Welfare Subjects and Autopoiesis | Bruckner (2025), DOI-10.1017/apa.2025.10006. Bruckner proposes, by abduction and not deduction (§4), that being autopoietic is sufficient, not necessary, for being a welfare subject. An entity is autopoietic when it "sustains, maintains, and renews itself in a way that responds and adapts to its environmental conditions". On this view insentient plants and a hypothetical non-sentient self-maintaining car ("Tessler") are welfare subjects, while engines with governors, thermostats and heat-seeking missiles are not. He answers the charge of absurd obligations in two ways: welfare value may not generate agent-neutral reasons at all, and if it does, the reasons concerning non-conscious subjects are "extremely weak" (Bradford 2023). | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-093](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-093.md)); worth reading as the clearest short statement of a welfare criterion that is not based on sentience and admits machines. | [LIT-143](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-143.md) | What is a Mathematical Structure of Conscious Experience? | Kleiner et al. (2023), [ARXIV-2301.11812](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.11812). Saying that a mathematical structure "describes" experience is not enough, since it admits incompatible, arbitrarily redefined and consciousness-indifferent structures. A structure S is *of* conscious experience only if experience has an "S-aspect" — one that a variation of experience changes exactly when the variation fails to preserve S. On this test relative similarity and topology (via phenomenal unity) qualify and metric spaces do not. | Deferred — seeded from the abstract and a skim on 2026-09-26; not read in full |
| [LIT-146](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-146.md) v2 | The Moral Status of Animals | Gruen & Monsó (2003), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/moral-animal/>. The entry reviews five proposed grounds of moral considerability (species membership, human-exceptional capacities, personhood, sentience and agency). Its conclusion is that attempts to establish human uniqueness by capacities are "not the most promising" (§1.2). It then separates *having* moral status from the *weight* of a claim ("showing up on a moral radar screen", §2.2). Weight depends on the value theory adopted for animal interests (hedonism, preference satisfaction, objective list; §2.1) and on the normative framework (rights, which are absolute but generate forward-looking duties when violated, or a multi-factor utilitarianism). It closes with virtue-ethical, feminist, relational and empathy-based approaches that reject argument from capacities altogether (§3). | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-181](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-181.md)); worth reading as the standard current survey of the grounds and weighing of animals' moral status. It is balanced for most of its length, but §2.2 argues at length for a multi-factor utilitarian view and §3 ends on Gruen's own "entangled empathy", so cite it for the map, not as neutral on the weighing. |
| [LIT-159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-159.md) v3 | If materialism is true, the United States is probably conscious | Schwitzgebel (2014), DOI-10.1007/s11098-014-0387-8. A conditional, informal argument. Any materialist criterion liberal enough to credit rabbits (and rabbit-level distributed aliens, the "squidbits") and behaviourally human-like but oddly built aliens (Sirian supersquids, Antarean antheads) with consciousness also credits the United States. On this argument the US meets the usual materialist marks of consciousness: sophisticated information processing (roughly 10^14 person-to-person visual "connections", comparable to the brain's about 10^14 synapses), goal-directed environmental responsiveness, self-representation and historical embedding. The only exits are eliminativism, extreme sparseness or neurochauvinism, each costlier than the conclusion. The paper argues for no universal criterion. It ends undecided between three readings: US consciousness, a challenge to materialists, or grounds to distrust universal metaphysics of mind. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-131](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-131.md)); read in full (manuscript) 2026-09-26; the canonical over-generation argument against liberal materialist criteria of consciousness, and the standard critique of anti-nesting and exclusion principles, worth reading for anyone who attributes consciousness from functional or indicator properties. |

It concludes that the issue "overall appears to converge" on one view: LLMs model the world in some senses but "probably" lack coherent causal world models, and are not likely paths to "artificial general superintelligence" (§1).
